ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two small balls of mass $m$ each with charges $+q$ and $-q$ respectively, are connected by a rigid massless rod of length $d$, forming a dipole. The dipole is parallel to the XY-plane and placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ perpendicular to this plane. Initially, the dipole is aligned with the X-axis and has an initial angular velocity $\omega_0$ in the XY-plane. Its center of mass is at the origin with an initial velocity $\vec{v}_0$ parallel to the XY-plane.

1. Given $\vec{v}_{0}=0$, find the minimal $\omega_{0}=\omega_{\text{min}}$ necessary for the dipole to reverse its orientation during the motion.
2. If the dipole starts with $\vec{v}_{0}=0$ and $\omega_{0}=\omega_{\text{min}}$ found in part (c), the trajectory of its center of mass has an asymptote. Find the distance $D$ from the origin to the asymptote.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, the dipole is located in the XY plane. Initially the rod is placed horizontally along the X axis, the left end is a negatively charged small ball, labeled -q,m, and the right end is a positively charged small ball, labeled +q,m. The distance between the two balls is labeled d. The coordinate origin is at the midpoint of the rod, the Y axis is vertically upward, and the X axis is to the right. The magnetic-field symbol is a circle with a dot, indicating that \vec B is perpendicular to the XY plane outward. The figure also draws the initial velocity of the center of mass \vec v_0 in the plane, and the initial angular velocity \omega_0 about the center of mass. Reasoning: Let the half-length of the rod be a=d/2, the center-of-mass coordinate be R=(X,Y), and the unit vector in the rod direction be n=(cosθ,sinθ), so the positions of the two balls are r_+=R+a n and r_-=R-a n. The kinetic energy of the system is T=m(\dot X^2+\dot Y^2)+m d^2 \dot θ^2/4. Take the symmetric gauge A=(1/2)B zhat×r, and the magnetic-field Lagrangian term is q A(r_+)·\dot r_+ - q A(r_-)·\dot r_-. Equivalently, after removing a total derivative, it can be written in the convenient form L=m\dot R^2+m d^2\dot θ^2/4+qBd\dot θ(X cosθ+Y sinθ). From the Euler equations of X,Y, translational conserved quantities can be obtained by integration. The initial conditions are \dot X(0)=\dot Y(0)=0, θ(0)=0, therefore \dot X=(qBd/2m)sinθ, \dot Y=(qBd/2m)(1-cosθ). Substituting them into the θ equation gives the effective one-dimensional equation of motion \ddot θ=-(qB/m)^2 sinθ. This is exactly a pendulum-type equation. The corresponding energy is (1/2)\dot θ^2+(qB/m)^2(1-cosθ)=(1/2)\omega_0^2. To just reverse to θ=π, the critical case is that the angular velocity is zero at θ=π, so (1/2)\omega_min^2=(qB/m)^2(1-cosπ)=2(qB/m)^2, therefore \omega_min=2qB/m; strictly speaking, take the magnitude as 2|q|B/m. In the critical case let Ω=qB/m, then \dot θ=2Ω cos(θ/2). At the same time \dot X=(Ω d/2)sinθ, \dot Y=(Ω d/2)(1-cosθ). Thus dX/dθ=\dot X/\dot θ=(d/2)sin(θ/2). Integrating from θ=0 to θ gives X(θ)=d[1-cos(θ/2)]. When θ→π, X→d; while dY/dθ contains a 1/cos(θ/2)-type divergence, so the trajectory of the center of mass approaches the vertical asymptote X=d. If the initial turning direction is opposite, then the asymptote is X=-d, but the distance from the origin to this line is still d.
